summary: This document defines the SVCB and HTTPS DNS record types, which tell clients how to reach a service before connecting. They can list multiple alternative endpoints with parameters such as transport settings, support future extensions like keys for encrypting the TLS ClientHello, and allow aliasing of a zone apex, which a CNAME cannot do.

plainLanguage.summary: These are new kinds of DNS record. Instead of just an IP address, they tell a client the addresses to try, which protocols the server speaks at each one, and which port to use. For HTTP there is a special variant that also says to use https.

how do https records work with http3
subtitle: DNS records that tell a client where to connect and how.

tldr.problem: A client that resolves only A and AAAA records learns only the IP addresses of a service, so it cannot know in advance which protocol to speak, which port to use, or that a better endpoint exists.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new DNS record types. SVCB lists alternative endpoints for a service with parameters attached to each, and HTTPS is a variant of it for HTTP origins that also signals that the scheme should be upgraded to https.
tldr.outcome: A client can learn the whole connection picture in one lookup, which saves round trips and can move traffic away from a service operator that is slow or far away. The records carry no authenticity of their own, so DNSSEC remains optional and clients must treat them as advice.

today: RFC 9460 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is still the definition of the SVCB and HTTPS record types.

sections.title: Why Another Kind of DNS Record
sections.content:
The SVCB and HTTPS resource records give clients complete instructions for accessing a service. The information enables better performance and privacy by avoiding transient connections to a suboptimal default server, negotiating a preferred protocol, and providing relevant public keys.

HTTP clients currently resolve only A and AAAA records for the origin hostname, learning only its IP addresses. If a client learned more about the origin before connecting, it could upgrade http URLs to https, enable HTTP/3 or Encrypted ClientHello, or switch to an operationally preferable endpoint. It is highly desirable to minimize the number of round trips and lookups needed to learn this extra information.

The records also help when the operator of a service wants to hand over operational control to other domains, for example aliasing the origin https://example.com to a service operator endpoint at svc.example.net. A CNAME can sometimes do this, but it does not cover all uses: CNAME is inadequate when the service operator needs to provide a bound collection of consistent configuration parameters through the DNS, such as network location, protocol and keying information.

The goals for the SVCB record are to provide alternative endpoints that are authoritative for the service along with parameters for each; not to assume that all alternative endpoints have the same parameters or capabilities, or are even operated by the same entity, since the DNS offers no way to tie several record sets together for one name; and to enable CNAME-like functionality at a zone apex, where CNAME is not allowed, and to extend operational authority for a service to other instances with alternate names.

The goals specific to HTTPS records include connecting directly to HTTP/3 alternative endpoints, supporting non-default TCP and UDP ports, enabling SRV-like benefits for HTTP where SRV has not been widely adopted, giving an indication that the https scheme should be used instead of http for all requests to a host and port, similar to HTTP Strict Transport Security, and enabling the conveyance of Encrypted ClientHello keys associated with an alternative endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal DNS answer says only where the server is. These records say what the server can do and which of several servers to prefer, so the client does not have to find out by trial and error.

sections.title: The SVCB Record and Its Wire Format
sections.content:
The SVCB DNS record type, type 64, is used to locate alternative endpoints for a service. It has two required fields and one optional one. SvcPriority is the priority of this record relative to others, with lower values preferred, and a value of 0 indicates AliasMode. TargetName is the domain name of either the alias target or the alternative endpoint. SvcParams is an optional list of key and value pairs describing the alternative endpoint at TargetName, used only in ServiceMode and otherwise ignored.

The zone-file presentation format is SvcPriority TargetName SvcParams. SvcPriority is a number from 0 to 65535, TargetName is a domain name, and the SvcParams are a whitespace-separated list of SvcParamKey=SvcParamValue pairs or standalone keys. Each key appears at most once, key names are lowercase alphanumeric strings of 1 to 63 characters from the ranges a to z, 0 to 9 and the hyphen, and parameters may appear in any order. Arbitrary keys can be written in an unknown-key format of keyNNNNN, where NNNNN is the numeric value of the key type without leading zeros.

On the wire, the RDATA consists of a two-octet field for SvcPriority in network byte order, the uncompressed fully qualified TargetName as a sequence of length-prefixed labels, and the SvcParams, which consume the remainder of the record. Each parameter is a two-octet key, a two-octet length between 0 and 65535, and an octet string of that length. Keys appear in increasing numeric order.

A client must treat a record as malformed if the end of the RDATA falls inside a parameter, if the keys are not in strictly increasing numeric order, or if a value does not have the expected format for its key. The second condition also rules out duplicate keys. If any records in a set are malformed, the client must reject the entire set and fall back to ordinary connection establishment.
sections.plainLanguage: The record holds a priority number, the name of the endpoint, and a list of settings. On the wire it is two bytes of priority, the endpoint name, and then the settings, each with its number and length.

sections.title: AliasMode and ServiceMode
sections.content:
The record has two modes. When SvcPriority is 0 the record is in AliasMode, otherwise it is in ServiceMode. All the records in a set should have the same mode, and if a set contains an AliasMode record, the recipient must ignore any ServiceMode records in it. Since record sets are unordered collections, SvcPriority imposes an ordering, and where several records share a priority clients should shuffle them randomly so that load is spread evenly.

In AliasMode the record aliases a service to a TargetName. An AliasMode set should hold only one record, and where several are present a client or resolver should pick one at random. The main purpose is to allow aliasing at the zone apex, where CNAME is not allowed. The TargetName will be a name that resolves to SVCB, AAAA and/or A records. Unlike CNAME, an AliasMode record does not affect the resolution of other record types and applies only to one specific service, not to a whole domain name. Any SvcParams present must be ignored, and the TargetName should not equal the owner name, which would loop.

In ServiceMode the TargetName and the SvcParams associate an alternative endpoint with its connection parameters. Each protocol scheme using SVCB must define a protocol mapping that explains how the parameters are applied, and unless the mapping says otherwise, clients must ignore any parameter they do not recognize. Some parameters impose requirements on others, and a record is called self-consistent when all its parameters comply with each other. Clients must reject any record whose recognized parameters are not self-consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: A record either says where the service really lives, or it describes one endpoint and how to talk to it. The first is for pointing a name at another name, the second for describing the alternatives.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
SVCB resolution is the process of enumerating and ordering the available endpoints for a service. The client takes the service name, adds the scheme prefix to form a query name, and issues a SVCB query. If an AliasMode record comes back, the query name becomes its TargetName and the client queries again, subject to chain length limits and loop detection. If one or more compatible ServiceMode records come back, they are the alternative endpoints and are sorted by ascending SvcPriority. Otherwise resolution has failed and the list of endpoints is empty. The procedure does not rely on any DNS server knowing about SVCB at all.

A client is SVCB-optional if it can connect without ServiceMode records, and SVCB-reliant otherwise. Clients for pre-existing protocols such as HTTP must be SVCB-optional. Such clients should issue any other DNS queries they might need in parallel, so that the delay is not worse when the record is absent. If at least one AliasMode record was processed, an SVCB-optional client appends an endpoint made of the final query name, the authority endpoint's port and no parameters, and tries the higher-priority alternatives first, falling back to lower ones. If connecting that way fails, an SVCB-optional client falls back to non-SVCB connection modes.

Resolution failures need care. If the DNS responses are cryptographically protected and SVCB resolution fails because of an authentication error, a SERVFAIL response, a transport error or a timeout, the client should abandon the attempt even if it is SVCB-optional, because an active attacker could otherwise mount a downgrade attack by denying the user access to the parameters. If the client enforces DNSSEC validation on A and AAAA responses, it should apply the same policy to SVCB, or an attacker could defeat that protection by forging SVCB responses pointing at other addresses. If the responses are not cryptographically protected, clients may treat failure as fatal or nonfatal.
sections.plainLanguage: The client looks up the record, follows any alias it points to, and then tries the endpoints in priority order. If the lookup fails in a way that suggests tampering, a careful client gives up rather than quietly falling back.

sections.title: The Initial Service Parameters
sections.content:
The alpn and no-default-alpn keys together indicate the set of Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation identifiers and associated transport protocols the endpoint supports. Clients filter that set against the protocols they support, and this informs the transport used, such as QUIC over UDP or TLS over TCP. The presentation value of alpn is a comma-separated list of identifiers, each a sequence of 1 to 255 octets. The presence of no-default-alpn means the default set of identifiers is not added; when it is present, alpn must also be present for the record to be self-consistent.

The port key gives the TCP or UDP port to use for the endpoint. If it is absent, clients use the authority endpoint's port number. The presentation value is a single decimal integer between 0 and 65535.

The ipv4hint and ipv6hint keys give IP addresses that clients may use to reach the service. If A and AAAA records for the TargetName are locally available, clients should ignore the hints, and otherwise they should query for those records and use the addresses that come back, because failing to do so can hurt load balancing and other location-aware features. The hints exist to reduce latency when a resolver is not compliant with the requirements, and should not be included if most clients use compliant resolvers.

The mandatory key lists the parameters a client must understand for the record to work. A ServiceMode record is compatible if the client recognizes all the mandatory keys and their values allow a successful connection; incompatible records are ignored. The key is always automatically mandatory and must not appear in its own value list.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings are the practical part: which protocols the endpoint speaks, which port to use, and which addresses to try. The mandatory key says which settings a client has to understand to use the record at all.

sections.title: The HTTPS Record for HTTP
sections.content:
Using any protocol with SVCB requires a protocol-specific mapping, and this section provides the mapping for the http and https schemes. To enable special handling for HTTP, the HTTPS record type is defined as an SVCB-compatible type specific to those two schemes. Clients must not perform SVCB queries or accept SVCB responses for the https or http schemes; they use the HTTPS record instead.

The presentation format is Name TTL IN HTTPS SvcPriority TargetName SvcParams. All the parameter keys defined for SVCB are permitted. The default set of ALPN identifiers is the single value http/1.1, and the automatically mandatory keys are port and no-default-alpn, so a client must either implement them or ignore any record where they appear. The presence of an HTTPS record for an origin also indicates that clients should connect securely and use the https scheme, which lets these records apply to existing http URLs while ensuring a secure and authenticated connection.

The query name for an HTTPS record uses Port Prefix Naming, with one modification: for the https scheme on port 443 the query name is the service name itself, with no prefix labels. Removing those labels enables offline DNSSEC signing of wildcard domains, which are common with HTTP, and lets the targets of existing CNAME chains start returning HTTPS records without the origin having to configure an extra delegation.

The record differs from HTTP Alternative Services in several ways. Unlike an Alt-Svc header value, an HTTPS record can list several ALPN identifiers. It carries no assurance of authenticity, since DNSSEC signing and validation are optional, so the resolution is modelled as an untrusted channel and there is no key corresponding to the Alt-Svc persist parameter. There is no key for the Alt-Svc max-age parameter either, because the expiry is expressed in the DNS TTL instead. And because the record is published for everyone, groups of clients necessarily receive the same settings, so it does not suit uses that need per-client tailoring.
sections.plainLanguage: The HTTPS record is the same idea with the web-specific parts filled in. It also tells the client to use https even when the user typed http, and it leaves out anything that would be unsafe to accept over an untrusted channel.

sections.title: Structuring the Zone
sections.content:
Each ServiceMode set can serve only a single scheme, indicated by the owner name and the record type, so zone owners must choose names that satisfy that constraint, including for alias and CNAME records. When using the generic SVCB type with aliasing, zone owners should choose alias target names that indicate the scheme in use, such as foosvc.example.net for foo schemes, and repeat the prefix labels when several ports are in use.

For performance, domain owners should minimize the use of AliasMode records and choose the TargetName by a convention the client knows, so the client can query for addresses in advance. The convention is to set TargetName to the service name for an initial ServiceMode record, or to the special name . when it is reached through an alias. Owners should avoid a TargetName below a DNAME, since that is likely unnecessary and makes responses slower and larger. Zone structures that require following more than eight aliases, counting both AliasMode and CNAME records, are NOT RECOMMENDED.

Some authoritative servers do not allow A or AAAA records on names starting with an underscore, which can be an operational problem when the TargetName contains such a label. The examples in the RFC cover a simple zone that adds a record telling clients the host speaks QUIC, an apex aliasing a domain to a server pool while the subdomain uses a CNAME, parameters bound to each server pool so a backup pool can use a different protocol and port, a multi-CDN configuration where different queries return different CNAMEs, and a non-HTTP use with an underscore-prefixed query name.
sections.plainLanguage: How the zone is laid out decides how quickly clients get an answer, so the RFC gives naming conventions to follow, including how to name an alias target so the client can guess it.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
These records permit distribution over untrusted channels, and clients are required to verify that the alternative endpoint is authoritative for the service, in the same way as for Alt-Svc. DNSSEC signing and validation are therefore optional for publishing and using them. Clients must ensure that their DNS cache is partitioned for each local network, or flushed on network changes, so that a local adversary cannot implant a forged record and then track users after they leave.

An attacker who can prevent SVCB resolution denies clients any associated security benefits. A hostile recursive resolver can always deny service to these queries, and network intermediaries can often prevent resolution even when the client and resolver validate DNSSEC and use a secure transport. Such downgrade attacks can prevent the https upgrade and disable other protections coordinated through the parameters, which is why clients are advised to abandon the attempt when an attack is detected. A hostile intermediary might also forge AliasMode records with the special name . to block particular services or protocols; clients that might be subject to this SHOULD ignore those records.

A hostile server can return records pointing at any address and port, including addresses inside the local network and ports assigned to internal services. If the attacker can influence the client's payload and an internal service has a lax parser, this could give access to that service. As a mitigation, mapping documents should indicate the port restrictions appropriate for the supported transports.

On privacy, ordinary address queries reveal the user's intent to reach a particular domain, which is visible to the resolver and to many other parties when plaintext DNS is used. A SVCB query additionally reveals the intent to use a particular protocol. That is not normally sensitive, but it should be considered when adding support in a new context.
sections.plainLanguage: These records are advice, not proof, so a client that trusts them blindly can be pushed to the wrong server. The RFC therefore says when a client should give up rather than fall back, and notes that the extra lookup reveals a little more about what the user is doing.

viz.caption: THE TWO MODES OF THE SVCB RECORD

cells: Delegates the service to another name
Binds an endpoint to its connection parameters
Aliasing a zone apex, where CNAME is not allowed
Listing endpoints with their protocols, ports and hints

items.label: mandatory
items.desc: The keys in this record that a client must recognize.

items.label: no-default-alpn
items.desc: No support for the default protocol.

items.title: Query the name
items.text: Ask for the record at the service name with the scheme prefix.

items.title: Follow any alias
items.text: If the answer is an alias record, query the name it points to, again.

items.title: Sort by priority
items.text: The alternative endpoints are sorted, lowest priority number first.

items.title: Try in order
items.text: Higher priority alternatives are tried first, with fallback to lower ones.

items.title: Fall back
items.text: A client that can work without these records falls back to ordinary lookup.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE FROM SECTION 10.4.3, WITH PARAMETERS BOUND TO EACH SERVER POOL

data.title: Zone with a primary and a backup pool
data.code:
$ORIGIN svc.example. ; A hosting provider
pool  7200 IN HTTPS 1 . alpn=h2,h3
              HTTPS 2 backup alpn=h2 port=8443
pool   300 IN A        192.0.2.2
                AAAA     2001:db8::2
backup 300 IN A        192.0.2.3
                AAAA     2001:db8::3
